entries.c74a9e29c77a089f6b93ad572a2779476581701a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8794"/><div sID="gen14618" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8794"/><hi type="bold">5. Or--</hi>Else; the only alternative, if Israel's enemies wish to escape being "burnt together."<div eID="gen14618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14619" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strength--</hi>rather, "the refuge which I afford" [Maurer]. "Take hold," refers to the horns of the altar which fugitives often laid hold of as an asylum (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.1.50">1Ki 1:50</reference>; 2:28). Jesus is God's "strength," or "refuge" which sinners must repair to and take hold of, if they are to have "peace" with God (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.24">Is 45:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.5.1">Ro 5:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.14">Ep 2:14</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Job.22.21">Job 22:21</reference>). <div eID="gen14619" type="x-p"/>
entries.7ea5bddc57737233d2ba0d0be4301891f37ea38b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8795"/><div sID="gen14620" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8795"/><hi type="bold">6. He--</hi>Jehovah. Here the song of the Lord as to His vineyard (<reference osisRef="Isa.27.2-Isa.27.5">Is 27:2-5</reference>) ends; and the prophet confirms the sentiment in the song, under the same image of a vine (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.92.13-Ps.92.15">Psa 92:13-15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.14.5">Ho 14:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.14.6">6</reference>).<div eID="gen14620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14621" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Israel ... fill ... world--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rom.11.12">Ro 11:12</reference>). <div eID="gen14621" type="x-p"/>
entries.5babd6bcae5d62482b8f8e97c98e95ea38eadbd9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8796"/><div sID="gen14622" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8796"/><hi type="bold">7. him ... those--</hi>Israel--Israel's enemies. Has God punished His people as severely as He has those enemies whom He employed to chastise Israel? No! Far from it. Israel, after trials, He will restore; Israel's enemies He will utterly destroy at last.<div eID="gen14622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14623" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the slaughter of them that are slain by him--</hi>rather, "Is Israel slain according to the slaughter of the enemy slain?" the slaughter wherewith the enemy is slain [Maurer]. <div eID="gen14623" type="x-p"/>
entries.0d8edbae9a67bc787abd0abadd65a5c33d0d983e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8797"/><div sID="gen14624" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8797"/><hi type="bold">8. In measure--</hi>not beyond measure; in moderation (<reference osisRef="Job.23.6">Job 23:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.6.1">Psa 6:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.10.24">Jr 10:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.30.11">30:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.46.28">46:28</reference>).<div eID="gen14624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14625" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when it shooteth--</hi>image from the vine; rather, passing from the image to the thing itself, "when sending her away (namely, Israel to exile; <reference osisRef="Isa.50.1">Is 50:1</reference>, God only putting the adulteress away when He might justly have put her to death), Thou didst punish her" [Gesenius].<div eID="gen14625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14626" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stayeth--</hi>rather, as Margin, "when He removeth it by His rough wind in the day," &c.<div eID="gen14626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14627" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">east wind--</hi>especially violent in the East (<reference osisRef="Job.27.21">Job 27:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.18.17">Jr 18:17</reference>). <div eID="gen14627" type="x-p"/>
entries.f8e9a4e3ee0878e3782c6b50cbc2ac5a807703fd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8798"/><div sID="gen14628" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8798"/><hi type="bold">9. By this--</hi>exile of Israel (the "sending away," <reference osisRef="Isa.27.8">Is 27:8</reference>).<div eID="gen14628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14629" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">purged--</hi>expiated [Horsley].<div eID="gen14629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14630" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all the fruit--</hi>This is the whole benefit designed to be brought about by the chastisement; namely, the removal of his (Israel's) sin (namely, object of idolatry; <reference osisRef="Deut.9.21">De 9:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.10.8">Ho 10:8</reference>).<div eID="gen14630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14631" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when he--</hi>Jehovah; at the destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar, His instrument. The Jews ever since have abhorred idolatry (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.17.8">Is 17:8</reference>).<div eID="gen14631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14632" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not stand up--</hi>shall rise no more [Horsley]. <div eID="gen14632" type="x-p"/>
entries.5c29eac5534efb1989f40d1c5584d63565752b70: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8799"/><div sID="gen14633" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8799"/><hi type="bold">10. city--</hi>Jerusalem; the beating asunder of whose altars and images was mentioned in <reference osisRef="Isa.27.9">Is 27:9</reference> (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.24.10-Isa.24.12">Is 24:10-12</reference>).<div eID="gen14633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14634" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">calf feed--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.17.2">Is 17:2</reference>); it shall be a vast wild pasture.<div eID="gen14634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14635" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">branches--</hi>resuming the image of the vine (<reference osisRef="Isa.27.2">Is 27:2</reference>,<reference osisRef="Isa.27.6">6</reference>). <div eID="gen14635" type="x-p"/>
entries.1b610bea9a0a10e6dad26c7e8d9e2874da3d7564: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8800"/><div sID="gen14636" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8800"/><hi type="bold">11. boughs ... broken off--</hi>so the Jews are called (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.17">Ro 11:17</reference>, 19, 20).<div eID="gen14636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14637" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">set ... on fire--</hi>burn them as fuel; "women" are specified, as probably it was their office to collect fuel and kindle the fire for cooking.<div eID="gen14637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14638" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no understanding--</hi>as to the ways of God (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.28">De 32:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.29">29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.5.21">Jr 5:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.4.6">Ho 4:6</reference>). <div eID="gen14638" type="x-p"/>
entries.594d65c7586814ceb293973dd882ac61f81504ab: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8801"/><div sID="gen14639" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8801"/>12. Restoration of the Jews from their dispersion, described under the image of fruits shaken from trees and collected.<div eID="gen14639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14640" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">beat off--</hi>as fruit beaten off a tree with a stick (<reference osisRef="Deut.24.20">De 24:20</reference>), and then gathered.<div eID="gen14640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14641" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">river--</hi>Euphrates.<div eID="gen14641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14642" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stream of Egypt--</hi>on the confines of Palestine and Egypt (<reference osisRef="Num.34.5">Nu 34:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.15.4">Jos 15:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.15.47">47</reference>), now Wady-el-Arish, Jehovah's vineyard, Israel, extended according to His purpose from the Nile to the Euphrates (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.21">1Ki 4:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.24">24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.72.8">Psa 72:8</reference>).<div eID="gen14642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14643" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">one by one--</hi>gathered most carefully, not merely as a nation, but as individuals. <div eID="gen14643" type="x-p"/>
entries.88dbb1c43550adf3d03a45652a02c100d296aa8e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8802"/><div sID="gen14644" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8802"/><hi type="bold">13. great trumpet--</hi>image from the trumpets blown on the first day of the seventh month to summon the people to a holy convocation (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.24">Le 23:24</reference>). Antitypically, the gospel trumpet (<reference osisRef="Rev.11.15">Re 11:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.14.6">14:6</reference>) which the Jews shall hearken to in the last days (<reference osisRef="Zech.12.10">Zec 12:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.13.1">13:1</reference>). As the passover in the first month answers to Christ's crucifixion, so the day of atonement and the idea of "salvation" connected with the feast of tabernacles in the same seventh month, answer to the crowning of "redemption" at His second coming; therefore redemption is put last in <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.30">1Co 1:30</reference>.<div eID="gen14644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14645" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Assyria--</hi>whither the ten tribes had been carried; Babylonia is mainly meant, to which Assyria at that time belonged; the two tribes were restored, and some of the ten accompanied them. However, "Assyria" is designedly used to point ultimately to the future restoration of the ten fully, never yet accomplished (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.18">Jr 3:18</reference>).<div eID="gen14645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14646" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Egypt--</hi>whither many had fled at the Babylonish captivity (<reference osisRef="Jer.41.17">Jr 41:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.41.18">18</reference>). Compare as to the future restoration, <reference osisRef="Isa.11.11">Is 11:11</reference>, 12, 16; <reference osisRef="Isa.51.9-Isa.51.16">51:9-16</reference> ("Rahab" being Egypt). <chapter eID="Isa.27"/>

entries.240cb08db62abf73b76ce063d164412bd7c6704c: <div eID="gen27554" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen27555" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27556" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27556" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27555" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27557" type="x-p"/> Destruction of the enemies of the Church, <reference osisRef="Isa.27.1">Isa 27:1</reference>. God's care of his vineyard, <reference osisRef="Isa.27.2-Isa.27.11">Isa 27:2-11</reference>. Prosperity of the descendants of Abraham in the latter days, <reference osisRef="Isa.27.12">Isa 27:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.27.13">Isa 27:13</reference>. <div eID="gen27557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27558" type="x-p"/> The subject of this chapter seems to be the nature, the measure, and the design of God's dealings with his people. <div eID="gen27558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27559" type="x-p"/> 1. His judgments inflicted on their great and powerful enemies, <reference osisRef="Isa.27.1">Isa 27:1</reference>. <div eID="gen27559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27560" type="x-p"/> 2. His constant care and protection of his favorite vineyard, in the form of a dialogue, <reference osisRef="Isa.27.2">Isa 27:2</reference>. <div eID="gen27560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27561" type="x-p"/> 3. The moderation and lenity with which the severity of his judgments have been tempered, <reference osisRef="Isa.27.7">Isa 27:7</reference>. <div eID="gen27561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27562" type="x-p"/> 4. The end and design of them, to recover them from idolatry, <reference osisRef="Isa.27.9">Isa 27:9</reference>. And, <div eID="gen27562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27563" type="x-p"/> 5. The recalling of them, on their repentance, from their several dispersions, <reference osisRef="Isa.27.12">Isa 27:12</reference>. <div eID="gen27563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27564" type="x-p"/> The first verse seems connected with the two last verses of the preceding chapter. - L. <div eID="gen27564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27565" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen27565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27566" type="x-p"/> Leviathan - The animals here mentioned seem to be the crocodile, rigid by the stiffness of the backbone, so that he cannot readily turn himself when he pursues his prey; hence the easiest way of escaping from him is by making frequent and short turnings: the serpent or dragon, flexible and winding, which coils himself up in a circular form: and the sea monster, or whale. These are used allegorically, without doubt for great potentates, enemies and persecutors of the people of God: but to specify the particular persons or states designed by the prophet under these images, is a matter of great difficulty, and comes not necessarily with in the design of these notes. R. D. Kimchi says, leviathan is a parable concerning the kings of the Gentiles: it is the largest fish in the sea, called also תנין tannin, the dragon, or rather the whale. By these names the Grecian, Turkish, and Roman empires are intended. The dragon of the sea seems to mean some nation having a strong naval force and extensive commerce. See Kimchi on the place.
entries.74c6a3f7553f6f22c0ed00779333247f708e7e88: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen27566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27567" type="x-p"/> Sing ye unto her - אנו לה anu lah. Bishop Lowth translates this, Sing ye a responsive song; and says that ענה anah, to answer, signifies occasionally to sing responsively; and that this mode of singing was frequently practiced among the ancient Hebrews. See De Poes. Sac. Hebrews Prael. xix., at the beginning. <div eID="gen27567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27568" type="x-p"/> This, indeed, was the ancient method of singing in various nations. The song was divided into distinct portions, and the singers sang alternately. There is a fine specimen of this in the song of Deborah and Barak; and also in the Idyls of Theocritus, and the Eclogues of Virgil. <div eID="gen27568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27569" type="x-p"/> This kind of singing was properly a dialogue in verse, sung to a particular tune, or in the mode which is now termed recitativo. I have seen it often practiced on funeral occasions among the descendants of the aboriginal Irish. The poems of Ossian are of this kind. <div eID="gen27569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27570" type="x-p"/> The learned Bishop distinguishes the parts of this dialogue thus: - <div eID="gen27570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27571" type="x-p"/> 3. Jehovah. It is I, Jehovah, that preserve her; I will water her every moment: I will take care of her by night; And by day I will keep guard over her. <div eID="gen27571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27572" type="x-p"/> 4. Vineyard. I have no wall for my defense: O that I had a fence of the thorn and brier! Jehovah. Against them should I march in battle, I should burn them up together. <div eID="gen27572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27573" type="x-p"/> 5. Ah! let her rather take hold of my protection. Vineyard. Let him make peace with me! Peace let him make with me! <div eID="gen27573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27574" type="x-p"/> 6. Jehovah. They that come from the root of Jacob shall flourish, Israel shall bud forth; And they shall fill the face of the world with fruit. <div eID="gen27574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27575" type="x-p"/> A vineyard of red wine - The redder the wine, the more it was valued, says Kimchi. <div eID="gen27575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27576" type="x-p"/> Bishop Lowth translates, To the beloved vineyard. For חמר chemer, red, a multitude of MSS. and editions have חמד chemed, desirable. This is supported by the Septuagint and Chaldee.
entries.c60ef2085c895350cfc8c43b7886510e5257b391: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen27576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27577" type="x-p"/> Lest any hurt it, I will keep it night and day - "I will take care of her by night; and by day I will keep guard over her" - For פן יפקד pen yiphkod, lest any visit it, the Syriac read ואפקד veephkod, and I will visit it. Twenty MSS. of Kennicott's, fourteen of De Rossi's, and two of my own, and six editions read אפקד ephkod, I will visit, in the first person.
entries.7c730ac5619c5e74622df6db2889b503bed9dbfa: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen27577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27578" type="x-p"/> Fury is not in me "I have no wall" - For חמה chemah, anger, the Septuagint and Syriac read חומה chomah, wall. An ancient MS. has חימה cheimah. For בה bad, in her, two MSS. read בם bam, in them, plural. The vineyard wishes for a wall and a fence of thorns - human strength and protection, (as the Jews were too apt to apply to their powerful neighbors for assistance, and to trust to the shadow of Egypt): Jehovah replies, that this would not avail her, nor defend her against his wrath. He counsels her, therefore, to betake herself to his protection. On which she entreats him to make peace with her. <div eID="gen27578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27579" type="x-p"/> From the above note it appears that the bishop reads, חומה chomah, wall, for חמה chemah, anger or fury, in accordance with the Syriac and Septuagint. The letter ו vau makes the only difference, which letter is frequently absent from many words where its place is supplied by the point. cholem: it might have been so here formerly; and in process of time both vau and cholem might have been lost. The Syriac supports the learned bishop's criticism, as the word shora is there used; which word in the plural is found, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.30">Heb 11:30</reference> : "By faith the walls of Jericho. "The bishop thinks the Septuagint is on his side: to me, it seems neither for nor against the criticism. The words in the Vatican copy are εγω πολις οχυρα, I am a fortified city; which the Arabic follows: but instead of οχυρα, the Codex Alexandrinus has ισχυρα, I am a Strong city. <div eID="gen27579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27580" type="x-p"/> The word חומה chomah, wall, is not found in any MS. in the collections of Kennicott and De Rossi, nor in any of my own MSS. <div eID="gen27580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27581" type="x-p"/> However, one of Dr. Kennicott's MSS. has חימה cheimah; but probably that which now appears to be a י yod was formerly a ו vau, and now partially obliterated. <div eID="gen27581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27582" type="x-p"/> This song receives much light from being collated with that in chap. 5.; and perhaps the bishop's criticism will find its best support from such a collation. In <reference osisRef="Isa.5.5">Isa 5:5</reference> of that chapter, God threatens to take away the wall of his vineyard: this was done; and here the vineyard complains, I have no wall, and wishes for any kind of defense rather than be thus naked. This is the only natural support of the above criticism. "About Tripoli there are abundance of vineyards and gardens, inclosed, for the most part, with hedges, which chiefly consist of the rhamnus, paliurus, oxyacantha, "etc. Rawolf, p. 21, 22. A fence of thorns is esteemed equal to a wall for strength, being commonly represented as impenetrable. See <reference osisRef="Mic.7.4">Mic 7:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.2.6">Hos 2:6</reference>. <div eID="gen27582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27583" type="x-p"/> Who would set the briers and thorns against me "O that I had a fence of the thorn and brier" - Seven MSS., (two ancient), and one edition, with the Syriac, Vulgate, and Aquila, read ושית veshayith, with the conjunction ו vau prefixed: Who would set the briers and thorns. מי יתנני שמיר שית mi yitteneni shamir shayith, Who shall give me the brier and thorn, i.e., for a defense: but hear Kimchi: "Who (the vineyard) hath given me (Jehovah) the brier and the thorn instead of good grapes."
entries.3c8f71157bad6d61539b31c4b4af75990f49ed2b: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen27583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27584" type="x-p"/> Or "Ah" - For או o I read אוי oi, as it was at first in a MS. The י yod was easily lost, being followed by another י yod.
entries.e184b529b67aff0b262c3ac8963d1f9914cdd540: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen27584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27585" type="x-p"/> To take root "From the root" - For ישרש yashresh, I read, with the Syriac, משרש mishshoresh. And for יציץ ופרח yatsits uparach, יציצו פרח yatsitsu parach, joining the ו vau to the first word, and taking that into construction with the first part of the sentence, Israel shall bud forth. I suppose the dialogue to be continued in this verse, which pursues the same image of the allegory, but in the way of metaphor.
entries.af33ea5f17dcc56ac146d34f0cd99d96d8baf39c: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen27585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27586" type="x-p"/> The groves "And if the groves" - ולא velo. Four MSS., two ancient, of Kennicott's, and one ancient of my own, with the Septuagint; this makes a fuller sense.
entries.a2bd0c48e4d4b9dd909e099fc458ad360bb7409c: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen27586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27587" type="x-p"/> There shall the calf feed - That is, the king of Egypt, says Kimchi.
entries.643380f57f9e18cd2c4002e55c7e12de10969c0f: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen27587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27588" type="x-p"/> The boughs thereof "Her boughs" - קציריה ketsireyha, MS. and Vulg.; that is, the boughs of the vineyard, referring still to the subject of the dialogue above. <div eID="gen27588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27589" type="x-p"/> The scarcity of fuel, especially wood, in most parts of the east is so great, that they supply it with every thing capable of burning; cow-dung dried, roots, parings of fruit, withered stalks of herbs and flowers; see <reference osisRef="Mat.6.21-Mat.6.30">Mat 6:21-30</reference>. Vine-twigs are particularly mentioned as used for fuel in dressing their food, by D'Arvieux; La Roque, Palestine, p. 198. Ezekiel says, in his parable of the vine, used figuratively for the people of God, as the vineyard is here: "Shall wood be taken thereof to do any work? or will men take a pin of it to hang any vessel thereon? Behold, it is cast into the fire for fuel; "<reference osisRef="Eze.15.3">Eze 15:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.15.4">Eze 15:4</reference>. "If a man abide not in one, "saith our Lord, "he is cast forth as a branch of the vine and is withered; and men gather them, and cast them into the fire, and they are burned;" <reference osisRef="Joh.15.6">Joh 15:6</reference>. They employed women and children to gather these things, and they laid them up in store for use. The dressing and pruning their vines afforded a good supply of the last sort of fuel; but the prophet says that the vines themselves of the beloved vineyard shall be blasted, withered, and broken, and the women shall come and gather them up, and carry away the whole of them to make their fires for domestic uses. See Harmer's Observations, vol. i., p. 254, etc.
entries.24ee519bb38db0ccad7aff6040dc581054290cfb: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen27589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27590" type="x-p"/> The channel of the river - The river Sabbation, beyond which the Israelites were carried captive. - Kimchi.
entries.2ec6303fd502ab386ebc09c95a8545926d0784bb: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen27590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27591" type="x-p"/> The great trumpet shall be blown - Does not this refer to the time spoken of by our Lord, <reference osisRef="Mat.24.31">Mat 24:31</reference> : He shall send forth his angels - the preachers of his Gospel with a great sound of a trumpet - the earnest invitation to be saved by Jesus Christ; and shall gather his elect - the Jews, his ancient chosen people, from the four winds - from all parts of the habitable globe in which they have been dispersed. <div eID="gen27591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27592" type="x-p"/> In this prophet there are several predictions relative to the conversion of Egypt to the true faith, which have not yet been fulfilled, and which must be fulfilled, for the truth of God cannot fail. Should Egypt ever succeed in casting off the Ottoman yoke, and fully establish its independence, it is most likely that the Gospel of Christ would have a speedy entrance into it; and, according to these prophecies, a wide and permanent diffusion. At present the Mohammedan power is a genuine antichrist. This also the Lord will remove in due time.  <chapter eID="Isa.27"/> <div eID="gen27592" type="x-p"/>

entries.53de1911f0d66d321951fe32b0ba72b3331f9613: <reference osisRef="Isa.27.1">Isa 27:1</reference> <div eID="gen13155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13156" type="x-p"/> Upon whom the judgment of Jehovah particularly falls, is described in figurative and enigmatical words in <reference osisRef="Isa.27.1">Isa 27:1</reference> : <hi type="italic">“In that day will Jehovah visit with His sword, with the hard, and the great, and the strong, leviathan the fleet serpent, and leviathan the twisted serpent, and slay the dragon in the sea.”</hi> No doubt the three animals are emblems of three imperial powers. The assertion that there are no more three animals than there are three swords, is a mistake. If the preposition were repeated in the case of the swords, as it is in the case of the animals, we should have to understand the passage as referring to three swords as well as three animals. But this is not the case. We have therefore to inquire what the three world-powers are; and this question is quite a justifiable one: for we have no reason to rest satisfied with the opinion held by Drechsler, that the three emblems are symbols of ungodly powers in general, of every kind and every sphere, unless the question itself is absolutely unanswerable. Now the <hi type="italic">tannin</hi> (the stretched-out aquatic animal) is the standing emblem of Egypt (<reference osisRef="Isa.51.9">Isa 51:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.74.13">Psa 74:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.3">Eze 29:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.2">Eze 32:2</reference>). And as the Euphrates-land and Asshur are mentioned in <reference osisRef="Isa.27.12">Isa 27:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.27.13">Isa 27:13</reference> in connection with Egypt, it is immediately probable that the other two animals signify the kingdom of the Tigris, i.e., Assyria, with its capital Nineveh which stood on the Tigris, and the kingdom of the Euphrates, i.e., Chaldea, with its capital Babylon which stood upon the Euphrates. Moreover, the application of the same epithet Leviathan to both the kingdoms, with simply a difference in the attributes, is suggestive of two kingdoms that were related to each other. We must not be misled by the fact that <hi type="italic">nâchâsh</hi> <hi type="italic">bâriach</hi> is a constellation in <reference osisRef="Job.26.13">Job 26:13</reference>; we have no <hi type="italic">bammarōm</hi> (on high) here, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.24.21">Isa 24:21</reference>, and therefore are evidently still upon the surface of the globe. The epithet employed was primarily suggested by the situation of the two cities. Nineveh was on the Tigris, which was called <hi type="italic">Chiddekel</hi>,<note placement="foot">In point of fact, not only does Arab. <hi type="italic">tyr</hi> signify both an arrow and the Tigris, according to the Neo-Persian lexicons, but the old explanation “Tigris, swift as a dart, since the Medes call the Tigris <hi type="italic">toxeuma</hi>” (the shot or shot arrow; Eustath, on Dion Perieg. v. 984), is confirmed by the Zendic <hi type="italic">tighri</hi>, which has been proved to be used in the sense of arrow or shot (<hi type="italic">Yesht</hi> 8, 6, <hi type="italic">yatha tighris mainyavacâo</hi>), i.e., like a heavenly arrow.</note> on account of the swiftness of its course and its terrible rapids; hence Asshur is compared to a serpent moving along in a rapid, impetuous, long, extended course (<hi type="italic">bâriach</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.43.14">Isa 43:14</reference>, is equivalent to barriach, a noun of the same form as עלּיז, and a different word from <hi type="italic">berriach</hi>, a bolt, <reference osisRef="Isa.15.5">Isa 15:5</reference>). Babylon, on the other hand, is compared to a twisted serpent, i.e., to one twisting about in serpentine curves, because it was situated on the very winding Euphrates, the windings of which are especially labyrinthine in the immediate vicinity of Babylon. The river did indeed flow straight away at one time, but by artificial cuttings it was made so serpentine that it passed the same place, viz., Arderikka, no less than three times; and according to the declaration of Herodotus in his own time, when any one sailed down the river, he had to pass it three times in three days (Ritter, x. p. 8). The real meaning of the emblem, however, is no more exhausted by this allusion to the geographical situation, than it was in the case of “the desert of the sea” (<reference osisRef="Isa.21.1">Isa 21:1</reference>). The attribute of winding is also a symbol of the longer duration of one empire than of the other, and of the more numerous complications into which Israel would be drawn by it. The world-power on the Tigris fires with rapidity upon Israel, so that the fate of Israel is very quickly decided. But the world-power on the Euphrates advances by many windings, and encircles its prey in many folds. And these windings are all the more numerous, because in the prophet’s view Babylon is the final form assumed by the empire of the world, and therefore Israel remains encircled by this serpent until the last days. The judgment upon Asshur, Babylon, and Egypt, is the judgment upon the world-powers universally.
entries.729bc2a810b8e088a837647786ef62d51a0a75a5: <reference osisRef="Isa.27.2-Isa.27.5">Isa 27:2-5</reference> <div eID="gen13156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13157" type="x-p"/> The prophecy here passes for the fourth time into the tone of a song. The church recognises itself in the judgments upon the world, as Jehovah’s well-protected and beloved vineyard.<hi type="italic">In that day a merry vineyard - sing it! I, Jehovah, its keeper, Every moment I water it. That nothing may come near it, I watch it night and day. Wrath have I none; O, had I thorns, thistles before me! I would make up to them in battle, Burn them all together. Men would then have to grasp at my protection, Make peace with me, Make peace with me. </hi> <div eID="gen13157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13158" type="x-p"/> Instead of introducing the song with, “In that day shall this song be sung,” or some such introduction, the prophecy passes at once into the song. It consists in a descending scale of strophes, consisting of one of five lines (<reference osisRef="Isa.27.2">Isa 27:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.27.3">Isa 27:3</reference>), one of four lines (<reference osisRef="Isa.27.4">Isa 27:4</reference>), and one of three lines (<reference osisRef="Isa.27.5">Isa 27:5</reference>). The thema is placed at the beginning, in the absolute case: <hi type="italic">cerem chemer</hi>. This may signify a vineyard of fiery or good wine (compare <hi type="italic">cerem zaith</hi> in Jdg 15:5); but it is possible that the reading should be <hi type="italic">cerem</hi> <hi type="italic">chemed</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.32.12">Isa 32:12</reference>, as the lxx, Targum, and most modern commentators assume.  ענּה ל signifies, according to Num 21:17; <reference osisRef="Ps.147.7">Psa 147:7</reference> (cf., <reference osisRef="Exod.32.18">Exo 32:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.88.1">Psa 88:1</reference>), to strike up a song with reference to anything - an onomatopoetic word (different from ענה, to begin, literally to meet). <hi type="italic">Cerem</hi> (the vineyard) is a feminine here, like בּאר, the well, in the song of the well in Num 21:17-18, and just as Israel, of which the vineyard here is a symbol (<reference osisRef="Isa.3.14">Isa 3:14</reference>; Isa 5:1.), is sometimes regarded as masculine, and at other times as feminine (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.20">Isa 26:20</reference>). Jehovah Himself is introduced as speaking. He is the keeper of the vineyard, who waters it every moment when there is any necessity (<hi type="italic">lirgâ‛im</hi>, like <hi type="italic">labbekârim</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.33.2">Isa 33:2</reference>, every morning), and watches it by night as well as by day, that nothing may visit it. על פּקד (to visit upon) is used in other cases to signify the infliction of punishment; here it denotes visitation by some kind of misfortune. Because it was the church purified through afflictions, the feelings of Jehovah towards it were pure love, without any admixture of the burning of anger (<hi type="italic">chēmâh</hi>). This is reserved for all who dare to do injury to this vineyard. Jehovah challenges these, and says, Who is there, then, that gives me thorns, thistles! עיתּנני = לי יתּן, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.9.1">Jer 9:1</reference>, cf., Jos 15:19.) The <hi type="italic">asyndeton</hi>, instead of ושׁית שׁמיר, which is customary elsewhere, corresponds to the excitement of the exalted defender. If He had thorns, thistles before Him, He would break forth upon them in war, i.e., make war upon them (<hi type="italic">bâh</hi>, neuter, upon such a mass of bush), and set it all on fire (הצית = הצּית). The arrangement of the strophes requires that we should connect כּמּלחמה with אפשׂעה (var. אפשׂעה), though this is at variance with the accents. We may see very clearly, even by the choice of the expression <hi type="italic">bammilchâmâh</hi>, that thorns and thistles are a figurative representation of the enemies of the church (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.6-2Sam.23.7">2Sa 23:6-7</reference>). And in this sense the song concludes in <reference osisRef="Isa.27.5">Isa 27:5</reference> : only by yielding themselves to mercy will they find mercy. או with a voluntative following, “unless,” as in Lev 26:41. “<hi type="italic">Take hold of:</hi>” <hi type="italic">hechezik</hi> <hi type="italic">b'</hi>, as in 1Ki 1:50, of Adonijah, who lays hold of the horns of the altar. “<hi type="italic">Make peace with:</hi>” <hi type="italic">‛âsâh</hi> <hi type="italic">shâlōm l'</hi>, as in Jos 9:15. The song closes here. What the church here utters, is the consciousness of the gracious protection of its God, as confirmed in her by the most recent events.
entries.d0dba3032ab6ed29f2ac59bfc19f8a51ab16b8b8: <reference osisRef="Isa.27.6">Isa 27:6</reference> <div eID="gen13158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13159" type="x-p"/> The prophet now adds to the song of the vineyard, by way of explanation. <hi type="italic">“In future will Jacob strike roots, Israel blossom and bud, and fill the surface of the globe with fruits.”</hi> We may see from הבּאים (<hi type="italic">acc. temp.</hi> as in <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.16">Ecc 2:16</reference>, equivalent in meaning to “Behold, the days come,” <reference osisRef="Jer.7.32">Jer 7:32</reference>, etc.), that the true language of prophecy commences again here. For the active וּמלאוּ, compare <reference osisRef="Jer.19.4">Jer 19:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.17">Eze 8:17</reference>, etc. The prophet here says, in a figure, just the same as the apostle in <reference osisRef="Rom.11.12">Rom 11:12</reference>, viz., that Israel, when restored once more to favour as a nation, will become “the riches of the Gentiles.”
entries.5e29140bd09f43e3b813a25614c50a345ed7a962: <reference osisRef="Isa.27.7-Isa.27.8">Isa 27:7-8</reference> <div eID="gen13159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13160" type="x-p"/> The prophet does not return even now to his own actual times; but, with the certainty that Israel will not be exalted until it has been deeply humbled on account of its sins, he placed himself in the midst of this state of punishment. And there, in the face of the glorious future which awaited Israel, the fact shines out brightly before his eyes, that the punishment which God inflicts upon Israel is a very different thing from that inflicted upon the world. <hi type="italic">“Hath He smitten it like the smiting of its smiter, or is it slain like the slaying of those slain by Him? Thou punishedst it with measures, when thou didst thrust it away, sifting with violent breath in the day of the east wind.”</hi> “<hi type="italic">Its smiter</hi>” (<hi type="italic">maccēhū</hi>) is the imperial power by which Israel had been attacked (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.20">Isa 10:20</reference>); and “those slain by Him” (הרגיו) are the slain of the empire who had fallen under the strokes of Jehovah. The former smote unmercifully, and its slain ones now lay without hope (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.14">Isa 26:14</reference>). Jehovah smites differently, and it is very different with the church, which has succumbed in the persons of its righteous members. For the double play upon words, see <reference osisRef="Isa.24.16">Isa 24:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.22.18">Isa 22:18</reference>; Isa 10:16. When Jehovah put Israel away (as if by means of a “bill of divorcement,” <reference osisRef="Isa.50.1">Isa 50:1</reference>), He strove against it (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.25">Isa 49:25</reference>), i.e., punished it, “<hi type="italic">in measure</hi>,” i.e., determining the measure very exactly, that it might not exceed the enduring power of Israel, not endanger the existence of Israel as a nation (cf., <hi type="italic">bemishpât</hi> in <reference osisRef="Jer.10.24">Jer 10:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.30.11">Jer 30:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.46.28">Jer 46:28</reference>). On the other hand, Hitzig, Ewald, and Knobel read בּסאסאה, from a word סאסא,<note placement="foot">Böttcher refers to a Talmudic word, הסיא (to remove), but this is to be pronounced הסּיא (= הסּיע), and is moreover, very uncertain.</note> related to זעזע, or even טאטא, “when thou didst disturb (or drive forth);” but the traditional text does not indicate any various reading with ה <hi type="italic">mappic.</hi>, and the ancient versions and expositors all take the word as a reduplication of סאה, which stands here as the third of an ephah to denote a moderately large measure. The clause <hi type="italic">hâgâh</hi> <hi type="italic">berūchō</hi> is probably regarded as an elliptical relative clause, in which case the transition to the third person can be best explained: “thou, who siftedst with violent breath.” <hi type="italic">Hâgâh</hi>, which only occurs again in <reference osisRef="Prov.25.4">Pro 25:4</reference>, signifies to separate, e.g., the dross from silver (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.25">Isa 1:25</reference>). Jehovah sifted Israel (compare the figure of the threshing-floor in <reference osisRef="Isa.21.10">Isa 21:10</reference>), at the time when, by suspending captivity over it, He blew as violently upon it as if the east wind had raged (vid., Job 2:1-13 :19). But He only sifted, He did not destroy.
entries.6dfc9f0d4199d70ca92e61709c266bbf5ebefc6d: <reference osisRef="Isa.27.9">Isa 27:9</reference> <div eID="gen13160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13161" type="x-p"/> He was angry, but not without love; He punished, but only to be able to pardon again. <hi type="italic">“Therefore will the guilt of Jacob be purged thus: and this is all the fruit of the removal of his son: when He maketh all altar-stones like chalk-stones that are broken in pieces, Astarte images and sun-pillars do not rise up again.”</hi> With the word “therefore” (<hi type="italic">lâcēn</hi>) a conclusion is drawn from the expression “by measure.” God punished Israel “by measure;” His punishment is a way to salvation: therefore it ceases as soon as its purpose is secured; and so would it cease now, if Israel would thoroughly renounce its sin, and, above all, the sin of all sins, namely idolatry. “Thus” (by this) refers to the בּשׂומו which follows; “by this,” namely the breaking to pieces of the altars and images of the moon goddess; or possibly, to speak more correctly, the goddess of the morning-star, and those of the sun-god as well (see <reference osisRef="Isa.17.8">Isa 17:8</reference>). By the fact that Israel put away the fundamental cause of all mischief, viz., idolatry, the guilt for which it had yet to make atonement would be covered, made good, or wiped away (on <hi type="italic">cuppar</hi>, see at <reference osisRef="Isa.22.14">Isa 22:14</reference>). The parenthesis (cf., <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.26.11">Isa 26:11</reference></hi>) affirms that this very consequence would be all the fruit (<hi type="italic">cŏl</hi>-<hi type="italic">peri</hi>) desired by Jehovah of the removal of the sin of Israel, which the chastisement was intended to effect.
entries.ed6550069bd95cda3bffd4c40407b1a16198f6be: <reference osisRef="Isa.27.10-Isa.27.11">Isa 27:10-11</reference> <div eID="gen13161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13162" type="x-p"/> The prophet said this from out of the midst of the state of punishment, and was therefore able still further to confirm the fact, that the punishment would cease with the sin, by the punishment which followed the sin. <hi type="italic">“For the strong city is solitary, a dwelling given up and forsaken like the steppe: there calves feed, and there they lie down, and eat off its branches. When its branches become withered, they are broken: women come, make fires with them; for it is not a people of intelligence: therefore its Creator has no pity upon it, and its Former does not pardon it.”</hi> The nation without any intelligence (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.3">Isa 1:3</reference>), of which Jehovah was the Creator and Former (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.11">Isa 22:11</reference>), is Israel; and therefore the fortress that has been destroyed is the city of Jerusalem. The standpoint of the prophet must therefore be beyond the destruction of Jerusalem, and in the midst of the captivity. If this appears strange for Isaiah, nearly every separate word in these two vv. rises up as a witness that it is Isaiah, and no other, who is speaking here (compare, as more general proofs, <reference osisRef="Isa.32.13-Isa.32.14">Isa 32:13-14</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Isa.5.17">Isa 5:17</reference>; and as more specific exemplifications, <reference osisRef="Isa.16.2">Isa 16:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.16.9">Isa 16:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.11.7">Isa 11:7</reference>, etc.). The suffix in “<hi type="italic">her</hi> branches” refers to the city, whose ruins were overgrown with bushes. Synonymous with סעפּים, branches (always written with <hi type="italic">dagesh</hi> in distinction from סעפים, clefts, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.21">Isa 2:21</reference>), is <hi type="italic">kâtzir</hi>, cuttings, equivalent to shoots that can be easily cut off. It was a mistake on the part of the early translators to take <hi type="italic">kâtzir</hi> in the sense of “harvest” (Vulg., Symm., Saad., though not the lxx or Luther). As <hi type="italic">kâtzir</hi> is a collective term here, signifying the whole mass of branches, the predicate can be written in the plural, <hi type="italic">tisshâbarnâh</hi>, which is not to be explained as a singular form, as in Isa 28:3. אותהּ, in the neuter sense, points back to this: women light it האיר, as in Mal 1:10), i.e., make with it a lighting flame (אור) and a warming fire (אוּר, <reference osisRef="Isa.54.16">Isa 54:16</reference>). So desolate does Jerusalem lie, that in the very spot which once swarmed with men a calf now quietly eats the green foliage of the bushes that grow between the ruins; and in the place whence hostile armies had formerly been compelled to withdraw without accomplishing their purpose, women now come and supply themselves with wood without the slightest opposition.
entries.2805a29ad3ba18f306cbdd8f3f89ecadbc97e09b: <reference osisRef="Isa.27.12-Isa.27.13">Isa 27:12-13</reference>  <div eID="gen13162" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Isa.27"/> <title type="x-s2">But when Israel repents, the mercy of Jehovah will change all this. <hi type="italic">“And it will come to pass on that day, Jehovah will appoint a beating of corn from the water-flood of the Euphrates to the brook of Egypt, and ye will be gathered together one by one, O sons of Israel. And it will come to pass in that day, a great trumpet will be blown, and the lost ones in the land of Asshur come, and the outcasts in the land of Egypt, and cast themselves down before Jehovah on the holy mountain in Jerusalem.”</hi> I regard every exposition of <reference osisRef="Isa.27.12">Isa 27:12</reference> which supposes it to refer to the return of the captives as altogether false. The Euphrates and the brook of Egypt, i.e., the <hi type="italic">Wady el-Arish</hi>, were the north-eastern and south-western boundaries of the land of Israel, according to the original promise (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.18">Gen 15:18</reference>; 1Ki 8:65), and it is not stated that Jehovah will beat on the outside of these boundaries, but within them. Hence Gesenius is upon a more correct track, when he explains it as meaning that “the kingdom will be peopled again in its greatest promised extent, and that as rapidly and numerously as if men had fallen like olives from the trees.” No doubt the word <hi type="italic">châbat</hi> is applied to the beating down of olives in <reference osisRef="Deut.24.20">Deu 24:20</reference>; but this figure is inapplicable here, as olives must already exist before they can be knocked down, whereas the land of Israel is to be thought of as desolate. What one expects is, that Jehovah will cause the dead to live within the whole of the broad expanse of the promised land (according to the promise in <reference osisRef="Isa.26.19">Isa 26:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.26.21">Isa 26:21</reference>). And the figure answers this expectation most clearly and most gloriously. <hi type="italic">Châbat</hi> as the word commonly applied to the knocking out of fruits with husks, which were too tender and valuable to be threshed. Such fruits, as the prophet himself affirms in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.27">Isa 28:27</reference>, were knocked out carefully with a stick, and would have been injured by the violence of ordinary threshing. And the great field of dead that stretched from the Euphrates to the Rhinokoloura,<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Rhinokoloura</hi> (or <hi type="italic">Rhinokoroura</hi>): for the origin of this name of the Wady el-Arish, see Strabo, xvi. 2, 31.</note> resembled a floor covered over with such tender, costly fruit. There true Israelites and apostate Israelites lay mixed together. But Jehovah would separate them. He would institute a beating, so that the true members of the church would come to the light of day, being separated from the false like grains sifted from their husks. “Thy dead will live;” it is to this that the prophet returns. And this view is supported by the choice of the word <hi type="italic">shibboleth</hi>, which combines in itself the meanings of “flood” (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.3">Psa 69:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.16">Psa 69:16</reference>) and “ear” (sc., of corn). This word gives a fine dilogy (compare the dilogy in <reference osisRef="Isa.19.18">Isa 19:18</reference> and <reference osisRef="Hab.2.7">Hab 2:7</reference>). From the “<hi type="italic">ear</hi>” of the Euphrates down to the Peninsula of Sinai, Jehovah would knock - a great heap of ears, the grains of which were to be gathered together “one by one,” i.e., singly (in the most careful manner possible; Greek, καθεῖς κατη ̓ ἓνα). To this risen church there would be added the still living <hi type="italic">diaspora</hi>, gathered together by the signal of God (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.18.3">Isa 18:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.11.12">Isa 11:12</reference>). Asshur and Egypt are named as lands of banishment. They represent all the lands of exile, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.19.23-Isa.19.25">Isa 19:23-25</reference> (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.11.11">Isa 11:11</reference>). The two names are emblematical, and therefore not to be used as proofs that the prophecy is within the range of Isaiah’s horizon. Nor is there any necessity for this. It is just as certain that the cycle of prophecy in chapters 24-27 belongs to Isaiah, and not to any other prophet, as it is that there are not two men to be found in the world with faces exactly alike.</title>
